artworks.title: Santhal Maiden
artworks.description: The collection of NGMA has close to 390 artworks of Mukul Dey which include drawings, sketches and prints acquired by the museum from the artist's family and from other private art collections. The artist's works include portraits and drawings of the renowned personalities of the time from diverse fields of politics, literature, science, education and also of the leading entrepreneurs, acquaintances, family members and friends. Apart from the portraits the collection also has paintings executed in the Bengal School style portraying landscapes especially of the Bengal countryside, the native people in all their glory, the flora and fauna, the saints and Bauls preaching wisdom through the villages, the monuments and also those narrating the religious fables, the folk tales and customs of the land. Mukul Dey mastered the technical nuances of the western print making process to express the romanticism and mysticism of the Indian culture. His stay at Santiniketan was particularly fruitful in the backdrop of the naturalistic surroundings of the place which is amply reflected in some of his early sketches. The above aquatint print is one such example showing a cut-out figure of a woman, titled as a santhal maiden by the artist, in a monochromatic black and white landscape.

metadata.inscription: The print bears an inscription '47.110/2243' at the bottom right corner of the painting with pen.

artworks.description: A known sculptor and a printmaker from Bengal, Somnath Hore has a typical style of rendering the forms and figures in his works. With time through his artistic practice, his human figures became simplified and shed details. with this reduction he achieved his individual style of contorted and suffering figures created with a mastered use of line. This etching print is a fine example of Hore's figures used n his works.

artworks.title: Untitled, 1967
artworks.description: Hore's work are filled by humanist eye, inclination towards empathy, and his communist ideology. Tension in lines and emaciating figures were significant in most of his works. He was driven with the feeling of anguished and suffering of the poor. The overall impression one gets from Somnath’s works is the depth of poverty he has starved in. He used knives and red-hot rods to cut and burn into a piece of clay, which then provided the basis for a cement mould that would shape and scar the paper pulp. He moulded the white paper to form wound-like gashes, and stained them with red blood-like pigment. The haunted imagery, blisters of the restrained figures made him poignant among others. Hore stated,' I do not make pictures, I make 'wounds' indeed.

artworks.title: Introspection - 21
artworks.description: Rajeev Lochan devised a unique style of working on photographs by adding strokes or blurring certain areas to create a unique and personal interpretation of the reality that the image captures. His earlier works on canvas were scenes of man-made surroundings devoid of human presence, reflecting apathy and neglect. He also painted photographs he took of ruins and ancient cities which were left desolate by time. His later work series titled `The Reality of Vision` drew out from these pictures of ruins, worked in mixed media on silver gelatine prints, which include solitary human figures posing in the midst of the debris of society. This work titled Introspection-21 is a fine experimentation with monochromatic medium.

artworks.title: Ceremony of unmasking
artworks.description: In ‘The Ceremony of Unmasking’ we see a woman flanked by two men in masks in the right panel while the left panel shows a masked man standing with his arms akimbo. In the middle panel of the triptych is a dog, next to a blue skull. The masked man in the left panel looks confident, in control and unperturbed. This is in contrast to the sense of apprehension that we see in the woman on the right panel, whose mask is being taken off by the man standing behind her. The sense of foreboding that runs through the work is heightened by the presence of the blue skull. Human skull is often depicted in art as a symbolic reminder of the inevitability of death. Anupam Sud’s nudes are often portrayed without hair or any other cultural markers. This makes them, in a sense, universal. Many of Sud’s themes deal with psychological tension between the sexes. Here, for instance, we wonder why the men are allowed to hide behind their masks while the woman is not. Anupam Sud has been recognized as an influential contributor to the growth of printmaking in India. She received her early training in art at the Delhi College of Art and won a fellowship to London’s Slade School to learn advanced techniques in printmaking.

artworks.description: Hore's work are filled by humanist eye, inclination towards empathy, and his communist ideology. Tension in lines and emaciating figures were significant in most of his works. He was driven with the feeling of anguished and suffering of the poor. The overall impression one gets from Somnath’s works is the depth of poverty he has starved in. He used knives and red-hot rods to cut and burn into a piece of clay, which then provided the basis for a cement mould that would shape and scar the paper pulp. He moulded the white paper to form wound-like gashes, and stained them with red blood-like pigment. The haunted imagery, blisters of the restrained figures made him poignant among others.
